bibl.title: What is polypharmacy? A systematic review of definitions

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: THE DEFINITIONS THEMSELVES - a systematic review whose unit of analysis is not a patient or an outcome but a DEFINITION, counting how many are in use for one word and what each of them says
span.quote: Studies not only defined polypharmacy but also used associated terms to define the level of polypharmacy; including minor (8 studies, 7.3%), moderate (1 study, 0.9%), major (12 studies, 10.9%), hyper (2 studies, 1.8%), excessive (10 studies, 9.1%), severe (1 study, 0.9%), appropriate (1 study, 0.9%), rational polypharmacy and indiscriminate prescribing (1 study, 0.9%), persistent (1 study, 0.9%), chronic (1 study, 0.9%), and pseudopolypharmacy (1 study, 0.9%). As a result, a total of 138 definitions of polypharmacy and associated terms were obtained. There were 111 numerical only definitions (80.4% of all definitions), 15 numerical definitions which incorporated a duration of therapy or healthcare setting (10.9%) and 12 descriptive definitions (8.7%).

span.label: what polypharmacy means in the published literature, and whether any article distinguishes appropriate from inappropriate polypharmacy
span.quote: Only seven studies (6.4% of all studies) defined appropriate or rational polypharmacy, or recognised the distinction between appropriate and inappropriate medications [ 10 , 79 , 114 – 118 ]. These studies either defined polypharmacy using a brief description only ( n = 3) [ 79 , 115 , 117 ] or used a brief description and polypharmacy tools such as the Beers criteria and the Medication Appropriateness Index (MAI) ( n = 4 studies) [ 10 , 114 , 116 , 118 ].

span.label: 138 definitions of polypharmacy and its derived terms, extracted from 110 articles and classified as numerical only, numerical-with-duration-or-setting, or descriptive - with the full range of thresholds and the share of studies using each
span.quote: Studies not only defined polypharmacy but also used associated terms to define the level of polypharmacy; including minor (8 studies, 7.3%), moderate (1 study, 0.9%), major (12 studies, 10.9%), hyper (2 studies, 1.8%), excessive (10 studies, 9.1%), severe (1 study, 0.9%), appropriate (1 study, 0.9%), rational polypharmacy and indiscriminate prescribing (1 study, 0.9%), persistent (1 study, 0.9%), chronic (1 study, 0.9%), and pseudopolypharmacy (1 study, 0.9%). As a result, a total of 138 definitions of polypharmacy and associated terms were obtained. There were 111 numerical only definitions (80.4% of all definitions), 15 numerical definitions which incorporated a duration of therapy or healthcare setting (10.9%) and 12 descriptive definitions (8.7%).

span.label: critique
span.quote: While the most commonly used definition of polypharmacy is being on five or more medicines, definitions are variable, which can cause confusion for researchers as well as clinicians in practice. Numerical definitions of polypharmacy do not account for specific comorbidities present and make it difficult to assess safety and appropriateness of therapy in the clinical setting. There is a need for an internationally agreed definition of polypharmacy.

span.label: a term in universal clinical use whose threshold varies five-fold between studies, and whose users almost never notice
span.quote: Of the 110 studies included in the review, only one highlighted the inconsistencies in the definitions of polypharmacy in the literature. The authors of this study suggested that polypharmacy be defined as patients visiting multiple pharmacies which may be associated with safety concerns relating to potential outcomes such as medication duplication, drug-drug interactions and adverse effects [ 112 ].

span.label: systematic review to PRISMA: MEDLINE (Ovid), EMBASE and Cochrane plus grey literature, 2000 to May 2016, English only; three reviewers on inclusion, one extractor, a pre-defined extraction template, all authors reviewing the content analysis
span.term: systematic review to PRISMA: MEDLINE (Ovid), EMBASE and Cochrane plus grey literature, 2000 to May 2016, English only; three reviewers on inclusion, one extractor, a pre-defined extraction template, all authors reviewing the content analysis
span.quote: A limitation of this review is the inclusion of studies in English only which can cause information bias. While EMABSE, MEDLINE (Ovid) and Cochrane databases were searched, the absence of other databases such as Scopus could have introduced selection bias. Additionally articles from the year 2000 until present have been included. There may be clinically relevant definitions for polypharmacy which were added to literature prior to 2000 which have not been included in this review. While authors discussed the inclusion criteria and data being extracted, there is still the potential for confusion bias.

span.label: **138 DEFINITIONS OF ONE TERM AND ITS FAMILY, FROM 110 ARTICLES**: `a total of 138 definitions of polypharmacy and associated terms were obtained. There were 111 NUMERICAL ONLY definitions (80.4% of all definitions), 15 numerical definitions which incorporated A DURATION OF THERAPY OR HEALTHCARE SETTING (10.9%) and 12 DESCRIPTIVE definitions (8.7%).` The review's unit of analysis is the definition - the only paper in this corpus whose object of study is what we tag
span.quote: Studies not only defined polypharmacy but also used associated terms to define the level of polypharmacy; including minor (8 studies, 7.3%), moderate (1 study, 0.9%), major (12 studies, 10.9%), hyper (2 studies, 1.8%), excessive (10 studies, 9.1%), severe (1 study, 0.9%), appropriate (1 study, 0.9%), rational polypharmacy and indiscriminate prescribing (1 study, 0.9%), persistent (1 study, 0.9%), chronic (1 study, 0.9%), and pseudopolypharmacy (1 study, 0.9%). As a result, a total of 138 definitions of polypharmacy and associated terms were obtained. There were 111 numerical only definitions (80.4% of all definitions), 15 numerical definitions which incorporated a duration of therapy or healthcare setting (10.9%) and 12 descriptive definitions (8.7%).

span.label: AND THE THRESHOLD VARIES FIVE-FOLD: `there was variation with regard to the actual definition of polypharmacy, WHICH RANGED FROM TWO OR MORE MEDICATIONS TO 11 OR MORE MEDICATIONS. The most commonly used definition for polypharmacy was FIVE OR MORE MEDICATIONS DAILY, with 46.4% (n = 51) of studies using this definition.` **The modal definition is used by FEWER THAN HALF the studies**, so the majority of the literature disagrees with the majority definition
span.quote: There was a wide range of variability in the definitions of polypharmacy as well as associated terms such as minor, moderate and major polypharmacy. The most commonly used term was polypharmacy, but there was variation with regard to the actual definition of polypharmacy, which ranged from two or more medications to 11 or more medications [ 13 , 90 ]. The most commonly used definition for polypharmacy was five or more medications daily, with 46.4% ( n = 51) of studies using this definition [ 11 , 24 – 73 ]. The second most common definition for polypharmacy was six or more medications, with ten studies using this definition [ 10 , 74 – 82 ]. Only one study defined polypharmacy as the number of drug classes used by a patient [ 91 ].

span.label: **AND 109 OF THE 110 DID NOT NOTICE**: `Of the 110 studies included in the review, ONLY ONE HIGHLIGHTED THE INCONSISTENCIES IN THE DEFINITIONS OF POLYPHARMACY IN THE LITERATURE.` And that one study's own definition is not about the number of drugs at all - it defines polypharmacy as `PATIENTS VISITING MULTIPLE PHARMACIES to obtain medications`. **The only author who noticed the disagreement was using a different REFERENT from everyone else**
span.quote: Of the 110 studies included in the review, only one highlighted the inconsistencies in the definitions of polypharmacy in the literature. The authors of this study suggested that polypharmacy be defined as patients visiting multiple pharmacies which may be associated with safety concerns relating to potential outcomes such as medication duplication, drug-drug interactions and adverse effects [ 112 ].

span.label: AND THE NUMBER HAS NO STATED CLINICAL BASIS: `the clinical basis for using a numerical count such as five or more medications to define polypharmacy and the potential of this to rationalise medication use and optimise health outcomes IS NOT ELUCIDATED IN MOST STUDIES.` A threshold in universal use whose derivation is unstated wherever it is used
span.quote: However, the clinical basis for using a numerical count such as five or more medications to define polypharmacy and the potential of this to rationalise medication use and optimise health outcomes is not elucidated in most studies.

span.label: AND THE COUNT DOES NOT MEASURE THE THING ANYONE CARES ABOUT: `THE SPECIFIC NUMBER OF DRUGS TAKEN IS NOT ITSELF INDICATIVE OF APPROPRIATENESS OF THERAPY as all of the drugs may be clinically necessary and appropriate for the patient` - and one cited author goes further: `when each of the medications can be linked to practice guidelines for chronic conditions for a given patient, USING A NUMERICAL CUT-OFF TO DEFINE POLYPHARMACY BECOMES IRRELEVANT`
span.quote: It is commonly reported that as the number of prescribed drugs increases, so do the chances of adverse drug events and likelihood of harm [ 120 ]. However, the specific number of drugs taken is not itself indicative of appropriateness of therapy as all of the drugs may be clinically necessary and appropriate for the patient.

span.label: AND THE PROPOSED REPAIR IS A NEW TERM, NOT A BETTER NUMBER: `There is a clear need towards adopting the term `APPROPRIATE POLYPHARMACY` in order to DIFFERENTIATE BETWEEN THE PRESCRIBING OF `MANY` AND `TOO MANY` DRUGS instead of a simple numerical count of medications, WHICH IS OF LIMITED VALUE IN PRACTICE.` The literature's answer to an unusable threshold is a qualitative term - and only 6.4% of the 110 studies make that distinction at all
span.quote: There is a clear need towards adopting the term ‘appropriate polypharmacy’ in order to differentiate between the prescribing of ‘many’ and ‘too many’ drugs instead of a simple numerical count of medications, which is of limited value in practice

span.label: AND ADDING PRECISION DID NOT ADD AGREEMENT: `Whilst the addition of DURATION OF THERAPY OR HEALTHCARE SETTING to a count of medicines in the definition of polypharmacy provided MORE SPECIFIC definitions, IT DID NOT PROVIDE ANY FURTHER CLARITY OR CONSISTENCY.` A more precise definition is not a more agreed one - and the review says the extra precision came from `THE DISPENSING DATA AVAILABLE`, not from a clinical argument
span.quote: Whilst the addition of duration of therapy or healthcare setting to a count of medicines in the definition of polypharmacy provided more specific definitions, it did not provide any further clarity or consistency.

span.label: AND THE REVIEW DOES SYNONYMY ON ITS OWN COLLECTION: `SOME STUDIES USED DIFFERENT WORDING BUT CONVEYED THE SAME DEFINITION of polypharmacy. For example, the definitions `Co-prescribing multiple medications` and `Simultaneous and long term use of different drugs by the same individual` DESCRIBE POLYPHARMACY AS THE USE OF MULTIPLE MEDICATIONS CONCURRENTLY.` Two surface forms collapsed to one sense, by hand, inside a review of definitions
span.quote: Some studies used different wording but conveyed the same definition of polypharmacy. For example, the definitions “Co-prescribing multiple medications” [ 113 ] and “Simultaneous and long term use of different drugs by the same individual” [ 77 ] describe polypharmacy as the use of multiple medications concurrently.

span.label: AND A SUB-TERM IS FLAGGED AS UNDEFINED BY THE REVIEWERS THEMSELVES (Table 4): `Rational polypharmacy recognizes LEGITIMATE PRESCRIBING and indiscriminate prescribing suggests INAPPROPRIATE PRESCRIBING (THE TERMS `LEGITIMATE PRESCRIBING` AND `INAPPROPRIATE PRESCRIBING` WERE NOT EXPLAINED).` A definition built entirely out of two terms its own author leaves undefined - the literature's version of this project's rule that a definer never fixes their own terms
span.quote: Rational polypharmacy recognizes legitimate prescribing and indiscriminate prescribing suggests inappropriate prescribing (the terms “legitimate prescribing” and “inappropriate prescribing” were not explained)

span.label: AND THERE IS A NAME FOR THE RECORD DISAGREEING WITH THE WORLD (Table 4): `PSEUDOPOLYPHARMACY - Patients being recorded as taking MORE MEDICATIONS THAN THEY ARE ACTUALLY TAKING.` A data-quality problem promoted to a named clinical term, in a literature that cannot agree what the unmodified term means
span.quote: Pseudopolypharmacy Patients being recorded as taking more medications than they are actually taking

span.label: THE COUNT OF DEFINITIONS EXCEEDS THE COUNT OF PAPERS, AND THE REASON IS COINAGE: `Articles NOT ONLY DEFINED POLYPHARMACY BUT ASSOCIATED TERMS SUCH AS MINOR AND MAJOR POLYPHARMACY. As a result, A TOTAL OF 138 DEFINITIONS ... were obtained` from 110 articles. A field asked to define one term produces more terms, and each new term needs its own definition.
span.quote: Articles not only defined polypharmacy but associated terms such as minor and major polypharmacy. As a result, a total of 138 definitions of polypharmacy and associated terms were obtained. There were 111 numerical only definitions (80.4% of all definitions), 15 numerical definitions which incorporated a duration of therapy or healthcare setting (10.9%) and 12 descriptive definitions (8.7%)

span.label: AND THE DISTINCTION THAT WOULD MAKE THE TERM USEFUL IS DRAWN BY ONE ARTICLE IN SIXTEEN: `ONLY 6.4% OF ARTICLES CLASSIFIED THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN APPROPRIATE AND INAPPROPRIATE POLYPHARMACY, using DESCRIPTIVE definitions to make this distinction.` The 93.6% that count pills cannot express it - a numerical threshold has no place to put `appropriate`.
span.quote: Only 6.4% of articles classified the distinction between appropriate and inappropriate polypharmacy, using descriptive definitions to make this distinction

span.label: THE REVIEW'S OWN BOUNDS: `A limitation of this review is THE INCLUSION OF STUDIES IN ENGLISH ONLY which can cause information bias. While EMABSE, MEDLINE (Ovid) and Cochrane databases were searched, THE ABSENCE OF OTHER DATABASES SUCH AS SCOPUS could have introduced selection bias. Additionally articles from the year 2000 until present have been included. THERE MAY BE CLINICALLY RELEVANT DEFINITIONS FOR POLYPHARMACY WHICH WERE ADDED TO LITERATURE PRIOR TO 2000.` So 138 is a floor, and the count of definitions is itself bounded by a search
span.quote: A limitation of this review is the inclusion of studies in English only which can cause information bias. While EMABSE, MEDLINE (Ovid) and Cochrane databases were searched, the absence of other databases such as Scopus could have introduced selection bias. Additionally articles from the year 2000 until present have been included. There may be clinically relevant definitions for polypharmacy which were added to literature prior to 2000 which have not been included in this review. While authors discussed the inclusion criteria and data being extracted, there is still the potential for confusion bias.

span.label: AND ONLY 6.4% MAKE THE DISTINCTION THE REVIEW ARGUES FOR: `ONLY SEVEN STUDIES (6.4% OF ALL STUDIES) DEFINED APPROPRIATE OR RATIONAL POLYPHARMACY, or recognised the distinction between appropriate and inappropriate medications. These studies either defined polypharmacy using a brief description only (n = 3) or used a brief description AND POLYPHARMACY TOOLS SUCH AS THE BEERS CRITERIA and the Medication Appropriateness Index (n = 4).` The alternative to the number is a published list, and four studies used one
span.quote: Only seven studies (6.4% of all studies) defined appropriate or rational polypharmacy, or recognised the distinction between appropriate and inappropriate medications [ 10 , 79 , 114 – 118 ]. These studies either defined polypharmacy using a brief description only ( n = 3) [ 79 , 115 , 117 ] or used a brief description and polypharmacy tools such as the Beers criteria and the Medication Appropriateness Index (MAI) ( n = 4 studies) [ 10 , 114 , 116 , 118 ].

span.label: and the conclusion is a request rather than a result: `definitions are variable, WHICH CAN CAUSE CONFUSION FOR RESEARCHERS AS WELL AS CLINICIANS IN PRACTICE. Numerical definitions of polypharmacy DO NOT ACCOUNT FOR SPECIFIC COMORBIDITIES PRESENT and make it difficult to assess safety and appropriateness of therapy in the clinical setting. THERE IS A NEED FOR AN INTERNATIONALLY AGREED DEFINITION OF POLYPHARMACY.` Written in 2017; cruz-jentoft2010 wrote the same sentence about sarcopenia in 2010 and kirk2024 was still writing it in 2024
span.quote: While the most commonly used definition of polypharmacy is being on five or more medicines, definitions are variable, which can cause confusion for researchers as well as clinicians in practice. Numerical definitions of polypharmacy do not account for specific comorbidities present and make it difficult to assess safety and appropriateness of therapy in the clinical setting. There is a need for an internationally agreed definition of polypharmacy.

span.label: THE REVIEW'S OWN VERDICT ON ITS FIELD, IN ITS CONCLUSIONS: `POLYPHARMACY DEFINITIONS WERE VARIABLE. NUMERICAL DEFINITIONS OF POLYPHARMACY DID NOT ACCOUNT FOR SPECIFIC COMORBIDITIES PRESENT and make it DIFFICULT TO ASSESS SAFETY AND APPROPRIATENESS OF THERAPY in the clinical setting.` The dominant definition type is judged unfit for the clinical decision the term exists to inform.
span.quote: Conclusions Polypharmacy definitions were variable. Numerical definitions of polypharmacy did not account for specific comorbidities present and make it difficult to assess safety and appropriateness of therapy in the clinical setting
